newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazilian wheat growers demand more government aid.
newsitem.headline: Brazilian wheat growers demand more government aid.

text.p: Brazilian wheat output may drop sharply in 1997 unless the government makes conditions at auctions of domestic wheat more attractive to millers so they buy the current harvest, analysts and millers said.

Red tape, the poor quality of Brazilian wheat and a plentiful supply of good quality wheat from neighbouring Argentina have kept millers away from recent government subsidy auctions, said Lawrence Pih of Moinho Pacifico.
"Besides the enormous bureaucracy involved in the process...there is the pricing of the subsidy," Pih said.
In auctions millers bid for wheat not at an outright price but at a subsidy to the minimum price of 157 reais ($152).
The miller pays the government the minimum price minus the subsidy set at the auction while the government pays the farmer the full minimum price.
The advantage for the government is that it does not have to pay for the storage of wheat as in previous years, with the wheat passing directly from the farmer to the mill.

Subsidies were around 16 reais ($15.69) in the most recent auction. In all, only 20,679 tonnes of wheat have been sold of the 600,000 tonnes offered since November, according to Banco do Brasil which handles the auctions.
"I have suggested that anything between 20 and 30 reais ($19.6 to 29.4) would be more palatable," said Pih.
Farmers in the key growing state of Parana are meeting tomorrow with the Agriculture Minister and representatives from the Banco do Brasil to discuss the problems with sales.
One suggestion is to extend the payment period to 180 days from the current five days, said Joao Paulo Koslovski, president of the Parana state cooperatives organisation (Ocepar).
"Payment terms for Argentine wheat are up to 360 days with eight percent interest rates a year," Koslovski said.
Farmers also want the government to reinstate mechanisms used in previous years when growers received financing for 180 days to allow them more time to sell their produce.
Pih predicted Brazil would buy six million tonnes from its Mercosur partner Argentina in 1997, leaving Brazil with excess domestic supply.
"There will be a situation of excess under any circumstances," he said.
He predicted that, with ample global supply forecast to keep prices low, Brazilian production would drop sharply in 1997.
"It will probably be a substantial reduction," Pih said.
Independent consultants Safras e Mercado have forecast that the 1997 harvest will fall to no more than two million tonnes after doubling to 3.13 million tonnes in 1996.
The anticipated drop is due to low prices and the subsequent lack of liquidity, Safras said in its weekly report.
